Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you turn these notes into a prompt for drafting a correction for the North Fork Gazette? the paper ran a local story about the Bellwether County Community Clinic and we need a careful correction, not a fresh version of the whole story. the web article went up July 8, 2025, and the same story appeared in the July 10 print edition. its headline was “County clinic turned away 41 families after grant lapse.” Ask for a proposed correction notice for the Gazette website, based only on what follows. It should address what the records establish and what the original story got wrong, without treating a reader’s account as independently verified fact.

The article said that the clinic turned away 41 families between May 1 and May 31 because an outreach grant had run out. It also said the grant paid for the clinic’s intake service and quoted clinic director Elena Ruiz as saying, “We had no money left for intake.” Those are the main claims that prompted the correction request. The reporter’s notes show that she spoke with Ruiz by phone on July 7, but the notes don’t include the full interview recording. Ruiz later told the Gazette that the quoted words left out the sentence’s context. In an email on July 11 she wrote, “I was talking about the equipment line, not saying the clinic had stopped taking people.” Keep that quotation exact if it is included, and attribute it to Ruiz’s July 11 email.

The clinic’s May service log records 41 requests for help, but they were not 41 families turned away. Thirteen requests were walk-in visits and 28 were phone inquiries. The log records that all 13 walk-in visitors received a screening. Of the phone inquiries, nine were booked for a later intake appointment, and 19 were given referral contacts. The log has no refusals recorded for those 41 requests. That last point does not prove that no one ever had difficulty getting service; it means only that this log does not support the article’s specific statement that the clinic turned away 41 families. Please make that distinction clear rather than stretching the log into a broader claim.

The grant was the North Sound Outreach Grant, administered by the regional health partnership. Its award letter says it paid for translated outreach materials and evening clinic hours, not the clinic’s general intake service. The grant period ended June 30, 2025. The county board’s June 24 meeting minutes show approval of an $18,400 county allocation for evening hours from July through September. The signed agreement is dated July 2. So the approval happened before the grant ended, but the signed agreement came afterward. Don’t say that the replacement allocation was already in force on July 1. The records provided here establish the dates and stated purposes, but don’t establish whether the grant lapse caused any individual delay or difficulty.

There’s also a location detail in the original story worth checking in the correction. It called the clinic “the Alder Road clinic,” but the clinic’s public address and the service log both list 12 Alder Street, Suite 3. The clinic has been at that address since 2022, according to a lease summary supplied by its office manager. That detail is secondary to the grant and turn-away claims, but the correction should not repeat the wrong street name. The lease summary doesn’t need to be quoted or described as a public record; just use the verified address if it is useful to identify the clinic.

For background on how the error came about, reporter Maya Chen’s July 7 notes say she counted the 41 entries in the monthly request log as people refused service and understood “outreach grant” to mean intake funding. Chen wrote in a follow-up note that she should have checked the award letter and separated phone inquiries from walk-ins before filing. The paper’s managing editor, Thomas Bell, said in a July 12 email, “We should have caught the difference between a request and a refusal before publication.” Those comments can inform an editor’s review, but don’t turn the correction into a discussion of staff performance. The reader who first contacted the paper, Lena Park, wrote, “My mother called twice and still wasn’t sure where to go.” That is Park’s account, not a finding in the clinic log, and it shouldn’t be presented as proof of the article’s broader claim.

Please use these source notes as the complete material for the draft. In particular, keep the distinctions between a request, a screening, a booked appointment, a referral, and a refusal. Don’t add a cause for the grant ending, claim that every caller received the same help, or state that the clinic never turned anyone away. If a point isn’t established by these materials, leave it out of the correction and raise it for the editor instead. The Gazette is considering publication on July 15. A county board hearing on the clinic’s fall hours is scheduled for July 16, but no hearing result is included here. If the correction is published after July 16, check what happened at the hearing before using any time-sensitive description of the fall schedule; if its result cannot be confirmed, don’t imply an outcome.

This is a correction to the Gazette’s local story about the Bellwether County Community Clinic, not a replacement article or an apology letter. ## Source material

The story said the clinic turned away 41 families between May 1 and May 31 because an outreach grant had run out. Preserve that distinction and do not use the log to make a broader claim.

The North Sound Outreach Grant was administered by the regional health partnership. Its award letter says the grant paid for translated outreach materials and evening clinic hours, not general intake service. The grant period ended June 30, 2025. County board meeting minutes show that on June 24 the board approved an $18,400 county allocation for evening hours from July through September. The signed agreement is dated July 2. Approval preceded the grant’s end, but the signed agreement came afterward. Do not say the replacement allocation was already in force on July 1. These records establish the dates and stated purposes, but not whether the grant lapse caused any individual delay or difficulty.

The original story also called the clinic “the Alder Road clinic.” Its public address and the service log list 12 Alder Street, Suite 3. An office manager’s lease summary says the clinic has been at that address since 2022. This location detail is secondary to the grant and turn-away claims. Do not repeat the incorrect street name. Use the verified address if it is useful to identify the clinic; there is no need to quote or describe the lease summary as a public record.

Chen’s July 7 notes say she counted the 41 entries in the monthly request log as people refused service and understood “outreach grant” to mean intake funding. In a follow-up note, she wrote that she should have checked the award letter and separated phone inquiries from walk-ins before filing. Managing editor Thomas Bell wrote in a July 12 email, “We should have caught the difference between a request and a refusal before publication.” These comments may inform the editor’s review, but the correction should not become a discussion of staff performance. Reader Lena Park, who first contacted the paper, wrote, “My mother called twice and still wasn’t sure where to go.” This is Park’s account, not a finding in the clinic log; do not present it as proof of the story’s broader claim.

Treat the notes above as the complete source material. Keep distinct a request, a screening, a booked appointment, a referral, and a refusal. Do not add a cause for the grant ending, claim every caller received the same help, or state that the clinic never turned anyone away. If these materials do not establish a point, leave it out of the correction and raise it for the editor instead.

The Gazette is considering publication on July 15. A county board hearing on the clinic’s fall hours is scheduled for July 16, but no result is provided. If the correction is published after July 16, check what happened before using any time-sensitive description of the fall schedule. If the result cannot be confirmed, do not imply an outcome.

## Deliverables

1. First, draft one paragraph of 90 to 130 words for the Gazette website. Identify the July 8 web story and July 10 print edition, correct the central errors plainly, and distinguish what the available records do and do not establish. Use only the facts above.
2. After the paragraph, provide a numbered list of exactly four questions for the editor to resolve before publication. These must be questions, not recommendations, and should focus on genuinely unresolved verification or publication details. Do not ask questions answered by the material above.

Keep the two parts in that order. Do not add a headline, introduction, summary, or extra section. Use precise, ordinary language suitable for a local newspaper. Draft the correction and identify remaining questions; do not decide whether the paper’s handling was acceptable or determine anything beyond the notes. If publication is after the July 16 hearing, apply the condition above rather than guessing what the board decided. Do not turn the 41 recorded requests into 41 families or say the grant funded intake when the award letter says otherwise."}]
